stages.name: Elasticity of supply of labour
stages.title: Elasticity of supply of labour
stages.sub: Explain why some jobs fill up quickly when wages rise, and others do not.

steps.q: A supermarket raises checkout wages by 10%. Within weeks, plenty of new people apply, since almost anyone can be trained on the till in a day. Now a hospital raises surgeon wages by 10%. Do surgeon numbers rise just as fast?
steps.right: No, far fewer new surgeons appear
steps.wrong: Yes, about the same number appear
steps.hint: Think about the qualifications needed to become a surgeon versus a checkout worker.

steps.q: Becoming a surgeon takes over 10 years of training, while becoming a checkout worker takes a day. If wages rise this year, which job can add new workers sooner?
steps.hint: Which job's training can actually be finished within the same year as the wage rise?

steps.q: Someone becomes a nurse mainly because they feel called to care for people, not chiefly for the pay. If nursing wages rise 10%, will many outsiders switch into nursing just for the money?
steps.right: No, few will switch in for pay alone
steps.wrong: Yes, many will switch in for the pay
steps.hint: Does a strong sense of vocation make people move in and out of a job purely because of wage changes?

steps.q: Given that surgeons need years of training and qualifications, respond slowly to wage changes, and often see the job as a calling, while checkout workers need almost none of this and respond fast, which job's labour supply is more sensitive to a wage rise?
steps.right: The checkout job's supply is far more sensitive
steps.wrong: Both jobs' supply are equally sensitive
steps.hint: Put the qualifications, training time and vocational factors together for each job.
